1. Metallurgical Processes & Furnace Scheduling Constraints
The cataloged literature spans the entire integrated steel production 
chain, from upstream liquid metal processing to thermal finishing 1-4:
•Upstream Steelmaking & Refining: Ironmaking via Blast Furnaces 
(BF) 1, melting in Basic Oxygen Furnaces (BOF) or Electric Arc 
Furnaces (EAF) 2, 3, secondary refining in Ladle Furnaces (LF) and 
Ruhrstahl-Hausen (RH) units 2, 3, argon oxygen decarburization 
(AOD) 2, and Continuous Casting (CC) 1, 3. 
•Reheating & Thermal Processing: Parallel walking beam 
reheating furnaces 5, 6, ingot soaking pits 7, 8, continuous gas-fired/
electric heat treatment flowshops 9-12, and ring forging furnaces 13. 
•Rolling Operations: Hot Strip Mills (HSM) comprising roughing and 
finishing mill stands 14, cold strip rolling 15, and steel powder 
manufacturing processes 16. 
•Energy & Utility Systems: By-product gas recovery (Coke Oven 
Gas COG, Blast Furnace Gas BFG, Linz-Donawitz Gas LDG), 
steam networks, turbogenerator power plants, and gas mixing 
stations 17-19. 
Core Furnace Scheduling Constraints:
1.Residence & Heating Requirements: Minimum and maximum 
heating/holding times parameterized by slab/billet dimensions, steel 
grades, and initial charging temperatures 20-22. 
2.Physical Kinematics & Interlocks: Strict First-In-First-Out (FIFO) 
material movement inside walking beam furnaces 20, 23, 
mechanical interlocks preventing simultaneous charging/stepping/
extracting 20, 24, furnace length capacity bounds 25, and laser point 
clearance constraints 25. 
3.No-Idle & No-Wait Rules: Rigid continuous processing rules ("no-
wait") between furnaces and cooling beds to prevent thermal 
degradation 10, 13, alongside "no-idle" constraints aimed at 
eliminating non-productive standby power consumption 12, 26-28. 
4.Technological Sequence Jump Limits: Restrictions on width, 
thickness, and hardness variations between adjacent slabs in rolling

2. Documented Operational Bottlenecks & System Limits
The literature explicitly identifies five major industrial bottlenecks that limit 
system throughput and energy efficiency:
•Thermal Degradation ("Deterioration Effect"): Ingot and slab 
cooling during transportation or buffer delays increases required 
heating times in furnaces, exponentially scaling fuel consumption 
and rolling resistance 33-37. 
•Ladle Logistics & Thermal Losses: In steelmaking-continuous 
casting (SCC), ladle turnover is a prime throughput constraint 38, 
39. Radiative/conductive heat loss through ladle linings (accounting 
for 40–50% of total heat loss) demands significant startup energy 
and continuous gas baking, creating severe trade-offs between fleet 
size and energy costs 40-43. 
•By-Product Gas Supply Volatility: Random generation rates of 
COG, BFG, and LDG combined with gasholder storage upper/lower 
bounds create frequent risks of gas flaring (waste) or fuel shortages 
at thermal plants 44-48. 
•Dynamic Disturbances & Cast Breaks: Unplanned machine 
breakdowns, hot metal release delays, and schedule disruptions risk 
triggering "cast breaks" (interruption of continuous casting), leading 
to major rescheduling costs and product degradation 49-52. 
•Electricity Spot Market & Peak Tariffs: Fluctuating Time-of-Use 
(TOU) tariffs and spot market dynamics restrict high-power 
equipment (e.g., EAFs, electric furnaces) to specific operational 
windows, requiring complex load shifting 8, 16, 53-55. 
3. Technological Tools & Methodologies
To address these complex, NP-hard combinatorial scheduling challenges, 
the archive provides a rich spectrum of advanced decision-support 
technologies 56-58: 

1.Exact & Mathematical Programming: Mixed-Integer Linear 
Programming (MILP) 10, 59, chance-constrained programming 60, 
polynomial-time shortest path transformations for bilinear furnace 
dynamics 26, 61, Benders' decomposition 62, and rolling horizon 
algorithms with Holt-Winters time-series forecasting 44, 63. 
2.Metaheuristics & Hybrid Matheuristics: Non-dominated Sorting 
Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) 64-66, Multi-Objective Particle Swarm 
Optimization (SA-MOPSO) 67, Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) 22, 
Enhanced Migrating Birds Optimization (EMBO) 68, Adaptive Large 
Neighborhood Search (ALNS) 69, and multi-objective matheuristics 
(MOVNS + MILP) 10, 70. 
3.Data-Driven & Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL): Multi-Agent 
Reinforcement Learning (MARL/MAPPO) with attention mechanisms 
for decentralized control 55, 71, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) combined 
with ALADIN decomposition 72, Branching Dueling Double Q-
Networks (BD3QN) 53, and Large Language Model-assisted DRL 
(HFLLMDRL) integrating Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) for 
dynamic reward shaping 73, 74. 
4.Digital Twins & Cyber-Physical Architectures: 5D Digital Twin 
models 5, Three-Stage Virtual Simulation Models (TSM) 5, Asset 
Administration Shell (AAS) interoperability standards 75, 76, and 
LightGBM rolling force predictors 77. 
5.Explainable AI (XAI) & Human-Centric Systems: Multi-objective 
counterfactual explanations utilizing Gower distance metrics 78-80, 
SHAP force plots for agent transparency 81, decision-tree 
visualizations 82, and Industry 5.0 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) / 
Intelligence Augmentation (IA) safety frameworks 1, 83.

1. Contrasting Methodologies Across the Archive
The literature reveals two fundamental methodological dichotomies reﬂecting intrinsic tensions 
between mathematical rigor, computational speed, physical ﬁdelity, and empirical approximation.
A. Deterministic Mathematical Optimization vs. Stochastic Deep Reinforcement 
Learning (DRL)
• Deterministic Solvers & Matheuristics: Exact mathematical formulations—including 
Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), Chance-Constrained Programming (CCP), 
Benders' Decomposition, and multi-objective matheuristics (MOVNS + MILP)—seek 
global optimality under explicit constraints. These methods provide mathematical 
guarantees for small-to-medium problem instances. However, because job-shop and ﬂow-
shop scheduling problems are NP-hard, computational time scales exponentially with 
problem size. When unexpected dynamic disruptions occur on the shop ﬂoor, re-running 
deterministic solvers online introduces high latency, often rendering the calculated schedule 
obsolete before execution.
• Stochastic DRL & Multi-Agent Systems: Deep Reinforcement Learning frameworks—
such as Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with ALADIN decomposition, Attention-Based POMDP 
formulations, Multi-Agent DRL (MAPPO/DDPG), and Deep Q-Networks (DQN)—shift the 
heavy computational burden ofﬂine. By simulating plant dynamics over millions of state-
action transitions, DRL agents learn a generalized policy π(a∣s) that executes online 
inference in microseconds to milliseconds. However, model-free DRL approaches lack 
explicit constraint enforcement mechanisms; without heuristic action-masking or constraint 
ﬁltering, policy-gradient methods can converge to poor local optima, exhibit high sample 
variance, or produce physically infeasible control actions.
B. Static Physics-Based Thermal Dynamics vs. Black-Box Data-Driven 
Approximations
• Physics-Informed & Kinetic Modeling: Control-theoretic and kinetic formulations—such 
as continuous bilinear system models governed by Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP), 
5D Digital Twins with Three-Stage Virtual Kinetics, and exact start-time-dependent slab 
deterioration functions—calculate energy consumption based on underlying thermodynamic 
laws. They account for continuous thermal losses, radiative heat transfer, and physical 
conveyor kinematics (FIFO interlocks). While highly accurate, embedding these continuous, 
non-linear physical differential equations directly into plant-wide combinatorial scheduling 
models severely increases mathematical complexity.

• Data-Driven Neural & ML Approximations: Supervised machine learning models—such 
as Genetic Algorithm-optimized Back-Propagation (GA-BP) neural networks, hybrid 
LightGBM rolling force predictors, and LLM-assisted reward shaping networks—bypass 
complex heat transfer equations by ﬁtting high-dimensional historical operational data. 
While these models capture empirical interactions across disparate plant parameters, they 
function as statistical black boxes. When operational conditions drift outside historical 
training distributions (e.g., severe ambient temperature shifts or rare steel grade batches), 
purely data-driven approximators can exhibit unpredictable error margins.
2. Core Industrial Trade-Off Dilemmas
Implementing automated planning and scheduling tools in heavy metallurgical processing requires 
navigating three mandatory operational trade-offs:
Dilemma A: Energy Cost Optimization vs. Refractory Lining & Asset Longevity
• The Operational Conﬂict: Mathematical algorithms designed to minimize energy costs or 
electricity spot market tariffs frequently dictate shutting down furnaces during idle gaps or 
rapidly modulating thermal power inputs between processing and standby states. 
Conversely, plant maintenance engineering requires maintaining stable thermal equilibrium 
to preserve refractory brick linings in heating furnaces, soaking pits, and transport ladles.
• Metallurgical & Kinetic Mechanisms: Refractory materials undergo cyclic thermal 
expansion and contraction during temperature ramps. Rapid cooling or aggressive on/off 
cycling induces severe thermal fatigue, surface spalling, and refractory wall cracking. In 
ladle dispatching operations, conductive heat loss through the ladle shell and lining accounts 
for 40%–50% of the total thermal loss of molten steel. Reusing a ladle with low residual 
refractory brick life (tp ) or dropping a reheating furnace temperature during a short idle 
window requires energy-intensive gas preheating to re-establish operating temperatures 
(e.g., 960°C). This additional fuel burn can negate the energy savings achieved during the 
idle window while accelerating refractory degradation.
